paragraphs: I suppose that men have reached the point where the obstacles to their survival in the state of nature prove stronger than the resources each individual has for staying alive in that state. That original condition can then no longer continue, and the human race would perish unless it changed its way of living.

But men cannot create new forces; they can only combine and direct the ones that exist. So the only way they have to preserve themselves is to form, by joining together, a sum of forces large enough to overcome the resistance. They must set these forces in motion through a single driving power and make them act in concert.

This sum of forces can arise only when several persons come together. But the force and liberty of each man are the chief instruments of his self-preservation. How can he pledge them without harming his own interests and neglecting the care he owes to himself? In terms of my present subject, this difficulty can be stated as follows —

“The problem is to find a form of association that protects and defends the person and property of each member with the full common force, and in which each person, though united with all the others, obeys only himself and stays as free as before.” This is the basic problem that the _Social Contract_ solves.

The terms of this contract are fixed so firmly by the nature of the act that the smallest change would make them void and useless. So even if they have perhaps never been formally declared, they are the same everywhere, and everywhere they are silently understood and accepted. They stay in force until the social compact is violated. Then each person recovers his original rights and goes back to his natural liberty, and he loses the conventional liberty he gave it up for.

Properly understood, these clauses can be reduced to one: the total transfer of each associate, with all his rights, to the whole community. For, in the first place, since each gives himself completely, the conditions are the same for everyone; and since they are the same for everyone, no one has any interest in making them burdensome to others.

Moreover, because the transfer is made without reserve, the union is as perfect as it can be, and no associate has anything further to claim. For if individuals kept certain rights, there would be no common superior to judge between them and the public. Each, being his own judge on one point, would ask to be his own judge on all. The state of nature would continue, and the association would inevitably become either ineffective or tyrannical.

Last, when each man gives himself to everyone, he gives himself to no one. And since he gains over every associate exactly the same right that he grants that associate over himself, he gets back the equivalent of all he loses, plus extra force to protect what he has.
If, then, we set aside everything in the social compact that is not essential to it, we shall find that it comes down to these terms —
_“Each of us places his person and all his power in common under the supreme direction of the general will, and, as a body, we receive each member as an indivisible part of the whole.”_

At once, this act of association replaces the individual person of each party to the contract with a moral and collective body. That body has as many members as the assembly has votes, and from the act it receives its unity, its shared identity, its life and its will. This public person, formed by the union of all the others, used to be called a _city_,[1] and is now called a _Republic_ or _body politic_. Its members call it the _State_ when it is passive, the _Sovereign_ when it is active, and _Power_ when they compare it with others like itself. Those who are associated in it are collectively called the _people_. Individually they are called _citizens_ insofar as they share in the sovereign power, and _subjects_ insofar as they are under the laws of the State. These terms are often confused and used for one another, but it is enough to know how to tell them apart when they are used with precision.

modern times. Most people take a town for a city and a townsman for a citizen. They do not know that houses make a town, but citizens make a city. This same mistake once cost the Carthaginians dearly. I have never read of the title of citizens being given to the subjects of any prince, not even to the ancient Macedonians or the English of today, although they are closer to liberty than anyone else. Only the French casually use the name of citizens everywhere, because, as their dictionaries show, they have no idea what it means. If they did, they would be guilty, in taking it, of the crime of _lèse-majesté_. Among them the name expresses a virtue, not a right. When Bodin wrote of our citizens and townsmen, he made a bad blunder by taking one class for the other. M. d’Alembert avoided that error. In his article on Geneva he clearly distinguished the four orders of men (or even five, counting mere foreigners) who live in our town, of which only two make up the Republic. No other French writer, to my knowledge, has understood the real meaning of the word citizen.
